extracted.intended_audience: K–12 math teachers and math educators interested in classroom practice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing math lessons that move away from rote, overly scaffolded exercises toward tasks that require students to formulate problems, think critically, and engage with real-world contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid paint-by-numbers classwork
rubrics_metrics.description: Today's math curriculum is teaching students to expect -- and excel at -- paint-by-numbers classwork.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not design lessons that hand students step-by-step procedures for every problem. Reduce overly scaffolded, formulaic tasks that train students only to apply procedures without understanding. Allow space for students to struggle and make decisions rather than following predetermined steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize problem formulation over routine solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Robbing kids of a skill more important than solving problems: formulating them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students how to identify what a problem is actually asking, how to translate real-world situations into mathematical questions, and how to decide what information and assumptions are needed. Emphasize the process of creating and defining problems as a core skill, not just executing solution procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use classroom-tested exercises that prompt students to stop and think
rubrics_metrics.description: Dan Meyer shows classroom-tested math exercises that prompt students to stop and think.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select or design tasks that are engaging, often contextualized, and open enough to require interpretation and sense-making (e.g., estimation, ambiguous or incomplete data, real-world scenarios). Aim for problems that provoke inquiry and discussion rather than immediate, mechanical computation.
